title: Music Then vs. Now
subtitle: Six answers to one question, and what each one cost.
objectives: Order the stages of music storage and delivery
Say what each stage gained and cost
Describe how OPM changed across the decades

cards.title: One question, asked for a thousand years
cards.text: How do you get a sound from the person making it to the person who wants to hear it? Every format is an answer to that, and each one gave something up.

cards.title: Each step traded something
points: **Notation** let music travel — and froze it.
**Recording** kept the performance — and made one take permanent.
**MP3** made it portable — by throwing audio away.
**Streaming** gave you everything — and you own none of it.

cards.title: Six buttons
cards.text: Tap each stage. The second line is what actually changed.

options: It was small enough to send
question.explain: It deliberately discards audio. Size beat quality.

cards.title: Four decades in four lines
cards.text: Original Pilipino Music is a label for where it came from, not a single sound.
points: **1970s:** the Manila sound, and rock in Filipino.
**1978:** Freddie Aguilar's *Anak* becomes an international hit.
**1990s:** band culture — the Eraserheads and the alternative wave.
**Now:** streaming and self-release, with no label needed.

cards.title: Electric cars had to be given a sound
cards.text: An engine's noise was a by-product. Then it stopped existing, and it turned out we needed it.
points: **An electric motor is nearly silent** at low speed.
**Pedestrians could not hear a car coming.**
**Since 2019 in Europe and 2020 in the US**, new EVs must emit sound.
**Designers now compose it.** Sound became a decision.

question.explain: Access, not ownership. The catalogue can change without you.

cards.title: A vinyl groove is a physical copy of the air
cards.text: It is the least abstract storage ever invented.
points: **The groove is a wiggle** cut to match the sound wave.
**A needle rides it** and wiggles the same way.
**You can see the loud parts** — the groove is wider there.
**Every play wears it down.** Contact has a cost.

cards.title: Game audio is the newest answer
cards.text: A game cannot store a finished performance, because the performance has not happened yet.
points: **Short pieces are stored** and assembled live.
**Footsteps change with the surface** under you.
**The music reacts** to what you do.
**Back to live music**, in a way — nothing is fixed.

terms.def: Writing music down as marks on paper.
Making a file smaller, often by discarding data.
Playing audio held on someone else's computer.
Original Pilipino Music — a label for origin, not a genre.

cards.title: A hundred years, left to right
cards.alt: A vinyl record, a cassette tape, a compact disc and a smartphone with earphones laid out in a row
cards.text: Groove, tape, laser, and nothing at all. Each one answered the same question.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Live, notation, record, CD, MP3, streaming — each traded something.
The MP3 won on size, not sound quality.
Streaming gives access, not ownership.
OPM says where music came from, not what it sounds like.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 3 MAPEH, Music strand. The week is built on one question — how does a sound get from a player to a listener — so that 'then versus now' stops being nostalgia and becomes a chain of trade-offs. The MP3 is the key example: it won on file size while deliberately discarding audio, which is a useful lesson about why technologies win. The electric-car lens is the week's best hook and is factually anchored: silent motors created a safety problem, and sound became something designers compose rather than a by-product. OPM is presented as a label for origin, since calling it a genre is the usual error.
discussion: Ask what each format gave up.
Ask what it means to not own the music you listen to.
Ask why an electric car needs a sound.
extension: Have him listen to the same song on a phone speaker and on headphones and describe the difference.
Have him find out which year the oldest music in his library was recorded.
misconceptions: "Newer always sounds better." The MP3 discards audio on purpose.
"Streaming means you own it." It is access only.
"OPM is a genre." It is a statement about origin.
